stories.headline: Update: Ukraine's Ousted Defence Minister Refuses Alternative Post, Demands Reinstatement
stories.summary:
Ukraine's former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has rejected President Volodymyr Zelensky's offer of the deputy prime minister role, insisting he wants his position as defence minister restored. In a statement to journalists Thursday, Fedorov said only three roles — president, defence minister, and commander-in-chief — truly determine the course of the war, and that he had a concrete plan to end the conflict that was being implemented before his removal.

Fedorov, 35, was ousted last week in a move that triggered mass street protests across Ukraine. Zelensky subsequently sacked commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi under protest pressure, but demonstrators have vowed to continue until Fedorov is reinstated. Fedorov has been credited with transforming Ukraine's armed forces through data-driven innovation and the Army of Drones initiative, and is widely praised for anti-corruption efforts.

Fedorov has already been replaced by Yevhenii Khmara, a former senior official at Ukraine's Security Service. Presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said discussions between Zelensky and Fedorov were still continuing and that it would be "inappropriate to disclose details at this stage," leaving the political standoff unresolved.

The crisis comes at a sensitive moment in the war, with Ukraine claiming a window of opportunity to pressure Russia through long-range strikes on logistics hubs. Fedorov's refusal of an alternative post deepens the political uncertainty around Ukraine's military leadership at a critical juncture.

stories.headline: Google and Tesla Shares Plunge as AI Spending Rattles Markets
stories.summary:
Shares of Alphabet, Google's parent company, fell more than 7% Thursday while Tesla's stock dropped 13.5%, after both companies reported negative free cash flow alongside commitments to spend hundreds of billions more on artificial intelligence infrastructure. It was the first time Alphabet had recorded negative free cash flow since going public in 2004, with the figure coming in at negative $5.9 billion for the quarter.

Alphabet now expects to spend as much as $205 billion this year on AI projects and infrastructure — a $15 billion increase from estimates given just three months ago. Tesla has outlined spending of up to $25 billion. Despite Alphabet's quarterly revenue rising 23% year-over-year to $119.8 billion, investors expressed concern about whether the enormous outlays will generate sufficient returns.

Alphabet's CFO Anat Ashkanazi said capital expenditures were almost entirely AI-related, with $45 billion spent in the second quarter alone — 60% on servers, 40% on data centres. CEO Sundar Pichai described the current moment as "early innings" and defended the spending as disciplined, arguing that demand for AI capabilities continues to outpace investment.

The sell-off reflects broader investor anxiety about the pace and scale of AI spending across major tech companies, with analysts noting a "healthy degree of scepticism" about whether returns will match the investment. The combined market-cap losses from both companies ran into hundreds of billions of dollars in a single session.

stories.headline: Vance Boelter Sentenced to Life in Prison for Shootings of Minnesota Lawmakers and Spouses
stories.summary:
Vance Luther Boelter, 58, was sentenced Thursday to two consecutive life sentences plus 40 years in prison for the murder of Minnesota state lawmaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, and for opening fire on another elected official, state Senator John Hoffman, and his spouse. All sentences are to be served consecutively.

The sentence was the result of a plea deal under which Boelter avoided the death penalty. The attacks shocked the state and the nation, representing one of the most violent targeted assaults on elected officials in recent American history. Hortman had served as Speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives.

The case drew national attention both for the prominence of the victims and for the premeditated nature of the attack, which prosecutors said was politically motivated. Boelter had pleaded guilty, and Thursday's sentencing formally closes the criminal proceedings against him.

stories.headline: South Africa Dismisses ICC Petition Over Migrant Attacks as 160,000 Foreigners Flee
stories.summary:
South Africa's foreign ministry has rejected as "opportunistic" a petition filed at the International Criminal Court by two Ghanaian nationals seeking an investigation into systematic attacks on migrants in the country. The petition argues the violence could constitute crimes against humanity and accuses the South African government of failing to prevent or punish those responsible. South Africa insists the petition does not meet the ICC's legal threshold and that its own legal system is capable of addressing the matter.

An AFP tally based on figures from migrants' home governments indicates that more than 160,000 people have left South Africa over the past two months, significantly higher than the South African government's own figure of 53,000 deportations and voluntary repatriations. Ghana, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, and Uganda have all organized flights or buses to repatriate citizens. Ghana claims one of its nationals was killed in the violence — a claim South African authorities deny.

Anti-migrant protest groups had set June 30 as a deadline for undocumented foreigners to leave, with demonstrators accusing migrants of exacerbating unemployment, crime, and the collapse of public services. The West African regional bloc ECOWAS condemned the attacks on Sunday, and the UN has warned against scapegoating migrants for South Africa's socioeconomic difficulties.

The dispute has elevated diplomatic tensions across the African continent. The ICC has not yet publicly indicated whether it will consider the petition, and South Africa's government maintains that the matter is one for its domestic legal institutions.

stories.headline: 19 Million Eggs Recalled Across Several States Over Possible Salmonella Contamination
stories.summary:
Midwest Poultry Services, L.P., a large-scale egg producer based in North Manchester, Indiana, has voluntarily recalled approximately 19 million eggs — 1,589,577 dozen white-shell and brown cage-free shell eggs — after possible Salmonella Enteritidis contamination was detected at two of its Texas farms. The FDA posted the recall notice on July 22, with affected cartons carrying sell-by dates between July 20 and August 17, 2026.

The recalled eggs were distributed to Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Arkansas, New Mexico, and Mississippi, sold at Kroger and Brookshire Grocery stores as well as smaller retailers. Affected cartons carry identifying codes P-1950 or 0840962 with a Julian Date between 157 and 184 printed on the side. The company said it is not aware of any confirmed illnesses linked to its products at this time.

Salmonella Enteritidis can cause fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps, and can be fatal for young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. The CDC notes symptoms typically appear six hours to six days after exposure; most healthy adults recover within a week without treatment, but vulnerable populations may require medical intervention. Consumers who purchased affected eggs are urged to avoid consuming them and can obtain a full refund from the place of purchase.

stories.headline: Nicaragua's Legislature Debates Barring All Opposition Parties from Future Elections
stories.summary:
Nicaragua's government-controlled National Assembly is debating legislation that would formally bar opposition parties from participating in elections, with a vote expected in the first week of August. The move follows a declaration by President Daniel Ortega that "there will be no more elections" for the opposition to contest power — remarks made in a speech marking the 47th anniversary of the 1979 Sandinista revolution.

Ortega, 80, who has governed since 2007, accused the opposition of being financed by the United States and "conspiring" to seize power. The head of the National Assembly, Gustavo Porras, confirmed legislators are working to ensure there will not be "even a crack" for the opposition to establish a foothold. The move follows a series of prior crackdowns in which opposition candidates were jailed, exiled, or stripped of citizenship before the 2021 presidential election, which Ortega won in a one-sided contest.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned Ortega's remarks as revealing the "true authoritarian nature" of his rule, saying Ortega and his wife and co-president, Rosario Murillo, had "abandoned even the pretense of popular consent." UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also condemned the proposal, stating that "people of all political viewpoints must be allowed to vote and run for office."

The proposed legislation would effectively formalize what critics say has long been Nicaragua's de facto reality. Ortega extended presidential terms to six years via constitutional reform passed unanimously by the National Assembly in November 2025 and named Murillo as co-president, positioning her to assume the presidency should he be declared permanently absent amid reports of declining health.

stories.headline: Chinese Woman Wins Fields Medal in Historic First
stories.summary:
A Chinese woman has won the Fields Medal, mathematics' most prestigious award, in what marks the first time a Chinese woman has received the honor. The Fields Medal is awarded only once every four years to mathematicians under the age of 40, and is widely considered the discipline's equivalent of a Nobel Prize.

The award comes amid broader debate over academic brain drain between China and the United States. While concerns have persisted that top Chinese scholars have been leaving for American institutions, the recognition arrives at a moment when several high-profile Chinese academics have in fact returned to China, with some citing an increasingly hostile environment for foreign-born researchers in the United States.

The milestone is seen as significant both for its representation of women in elite mathematics — a field long dominated by men — and as a marker of China's growing prominence in fundamental scientific research on the world stage.

stories.headline: FDA Convenes Hearings on Seven Popular Peptides for Weight Loss, Healing, and Longevity
stories.summary:
The Food and Drug Administration's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee opened two days of hearings Wednesday at its Silver Spring, Maryland campus to consider whether seven unapproved peptide substances should be added to the 503A Bulks List, which would permit their use in compounded prescription drugs. The peptides under review include BPC-157, TB-500, and five others proposed for uses ranging from ulcerative colitis and wound healing to opioid withdrawal, obesity, and cerebral ischemia. Though not FDA-approved, these substances are already widely available through wellness clinics, compounding operations, and gray-market online sellers.

The hearings reflect a growing tension within federal health policy: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has publicly voiced support for expanding access to peptide therapies, while FDA reviewers have raised concerns about limited evidence supporting the safety and effectiveness of the substances under consideration. Proponents argue that years of patient use suggest a promising safety profile and that the compounds address unmet medical needs.

The outcome of the advisory committee's recommendations will shape whether millions of Americans can legally access these therapies through regulated compounding pharmacies. Consumer demand is expected to remain strong regardless of the committee's findings, given the surge in public interest in peptides for weight loss, muscle building, and chronic disease management.

stories.headline: Secret Service Says Threat Investigations Up 40%, Surpassing 10,000 Cases This Year
stories.summary:
Secret Service Director Sean Curran told reporters Wednesday that the agency has opened more than 10,000 threat investigations so far in 2026, representing roughly a 40 percent increase compared to the same period last year. Curran described the threat environment as "off the charts" and "very volatile," warning that the surge is forcing the agency to deploy more agents and investigative resources to protect senior government officials.

The increase raises concerns about whether the Secret Service can sustain its protective operations without strain, particularly as it simultaneously prepares for high-profile events such as Friday's rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner. The agency has not publicly detailed the nature or targets of the threats driving the increase.

The disclosure underscores a broader pattern of heightened political tension in the United States. The Secret Service has faced scrutiny over its resources and readiness following high-profile security lapses in recent years, and the latest figures will likely renew congressional attention to the agency's funding and capacity.

stories.headline: Update: India's Modi Government Reaches Out to Youth Protesters as Hunger Striker Hospitalized in ICU
stories.summary:
Indian activist Sonam Wangchuk, the prominent face of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest movement demanding education reforms, has been admitted to the ICU at Medanta Hospital in Gurugram after 26 days on hunger strike, during which he has lost 11 kilograms. Wangchuk was forcibly removed from the protest site at Delhi's Jantar Mantar last Saturday but has refused all appeals from opposition MPs, celebrities, and Health Minister JP Nadda to end his fast.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi broke his public silence on the protests Wednesday, posting on X that "nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth" and announcing fast-track courts to address the exam paper leak scandal that sparked the movement. However, CJP spokespersons rejected the response as insufficient, arguing Modi was treating symptoms rather than root causes. The protests have drawn widespread public sympathy, with Bollywood figures and Sikh temples providing food, shelter, and medical aid to demonstrators.

The movement poses a significant political challenge for Modi's government, which has dominated Indian social media for 12 years but now faces a generation using the same platforms against it. A police crackdown on Monday's march to parliament left dozens of protesters and officers injured, further galvanizing the opposition and drawing international attention to the unrest.

stories.headline: Canada's Dairy Supply Management System Becomes Flashpoint in U.S. Tariff Standoff
stories.summary:
Canada's decades-old dairy supply management system — which uses production quotas, set pricing, and steep import tariffs of up to 300 percent on foreign dairy — has emerged as a central sticking point in U.S.-Canada trade negotiations, with President Trump citing it as justification for a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods set to take effect in August. Trump argues the system is "unreasonable" to American farmers who want greater access to Canada's 40-million-person market, particularly as U.S. dairy production has reached record highs that outpace domestic consumption.

Canadian officials have signaled the system is non-negotiable. Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette, whose province hosts Canada's largest dairy industry, stated flatly that supply management would not be on the table, while U.S.-Canada Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc called it "a cornerstone of Canada's economy." Described by analysts as the most powerful political lobby in Canada — one with cross-party support — the dairy sector has historically mobilized tractors and cattle on Parliament Hill to resist trade concessions.

The standoff puts Canadian politicians in a difficult position: conceding ground on dairy could provoke a fierce domestic backlash, while holding firm risks a damaging escalation in tariffs affecting a broad swath of Canadian exports. American dairy farmers currently have tariff-free access to only 3.5 percent of Canada's market, even as Canada imported $1.3 billion in U.S. dairy products in 2025.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Launches 12th Night of Strikes on Iran as Ceasefire Talks Collapse
stories.summary:
The U.S. military announced it was conducting a 12th consecutive night of strikes against Iran, with U.S. Central Command stating the attacks were designed to further degrade Iran's ability to threaten civilian mariners and commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump warned that the U.S. would destroy one bridge or power plant each time Iran fires on a ship in the strait, and said the U.S. has "no interest" in further talks until Iran is ready to engage "in a meaningful way."

Trump also announced the U.S. would soon strike near Pickaxe Mountain, an underground site adjacent to Iran's Natanz nuclear enrichment facility. The president attended a dignified transfer ceremony at Dover Air Force Base for four U.S. service members killed in the conflict — the third such ceremony since launching the war in February — calling it "one of the hardest things to do as a president."

Diplomatic efforts to salvage an interim ceasefire agreement, brokered through Pakistan, have collapsed. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking at the ASEAN foreign ministers' meeting in Manila, said Iran has been reaching out directly and indirectly seeking talks but has not kept prior commitments. Both sides are increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure, escalating concerns about the conflict's humanitarian and economic toll.

The active strikes and Trump's threats to expand targets represent a material escalation from prior coverage. The conflict is affecting global oil markets, with prices above $90 a barrel, and the Houthi blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea is compounding pressure on global energy supplies.

stories.headline: Update: Houthi Maritime Blockade Forces Tankers to Reverse Course in Red Sea
stories.summary:
At least seven oil tankers have made sharp U-turns near Yemen after the Houthi group announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia, according to ship-tracking data. The vessels, travelling to or from Saudi ports, reversed course following the embargo announcement, which warned ships that they "may be subject to targeting in any location within the operational reach" of Houthi forces.

The Red Sea has become a critical alternative shipping route since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the U.S.-Iran conflict. Analysts warn that Houthi action against Red Sea traffic could sharply drive up global energy prices by removing the last major Gulf oil export corridor. The EU's naval force in the region recommended that vessels linked to U.S., Israeli, or Saudi interests avoid the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden until the threat level decreases.

Maritime intelligence firm Kpler noted that before the embargo, roughly 20 vessels per day were transiting the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Defence analysts say any Houthi attacks would suppress all international traffic, not just Saudi-bound ships, significantly disrupting global trade. The development adds a new front to the already severe disruption to global shipping caused by the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Installs New Army Commander as Zelenskyy Moves to End Political Crisis
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has appointed 43-year-old Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi as the new commander-in-chief of Ukraine's armed forces, following the dismissal of the previous army chief amid a week of political turmoil. Drapatyi is from a new generation of Ukrainian generals who rose through the ranks during the war with Russia, having first distinguished himself during Russia's 2014 seizure of Crimea.

The reshuffle was prompted by a public rift between the outgoing army chief and the defense minister, both of whom lost their positions in a broader government reorganization. Zelenskyy acknowledged the crisis had prompted rejoicing in Russia and moved to draw a clear line under the instability. It remains uncertain whether the personnel changes will fully restore cohesion within Ukraine's military leadership.

Ukraine has made significant battlefield progress this year, and the political infighting had threatened to undermine those gains. Drapatyi's appointment is the concrete new development in this ongoing story, marking the first confirmed successor since the commander's firing was previously reported.

stories.headline: Update: France Evacuates 12,000 as Wildfires Spread Through Gironde Region
stories.summary:
Around 12,000 people, including approximately 10,000 tourists, have been evacuated from southwestern France as wildfires continue to spread through the Gironde region, days after two firefighters died near Bordeaux airport. More than 2,400 hectares of land have been destroyed, and the Gironde region remains under a red alert. Authorities have banned the use of internal combustion and electric engines in forested areas and closed a number of roads.

Further evacuations took place Thursday morning on the Lège-Cap-Ferret peninsula. French officials described conditions of rapidly spreading fire and thick smoke, with residents reporting ash and burned debris falling from darkened skies. No additional deaths have been reported as of Thursday, but some leisure sites in exposed forest areas face further closures.

In neighboring Italy, a firefighter died tackling a wildfire in San Cataldo, Sicily, where authorities reported more than 350 fires on the island. Sicilian civil protection officials said the fires had human causes, characterizing firefighting as increasingly a social and public order problem. The scale of the crisis across both France and Italy marks what French authorities have described as the worst fire season in the country since World War II.
